## 🎯 The task

Forecast **your series from Week 4** with exponential smoothing. The material is the Week 4 lecture,
*Exponential Smoothing*.

The order matters, and it is marked:

1. **Specify the model by hand first** — error, trend, season, damping — from your own plots.
2. **Then** let `AutoETS` choose, and compare.
3. **Decide** between the candidates on a rolling origin, not on one window.
4. Check what is left in the residuals, and submit the forecast with the model's own 80% interval.

ETS only: no ARIMA, no regression, no averaging with other methods. Those come later, on this same
series.

::: {.callout-important}
## This one counts

8 points. **Deadline: 23:59 today**, on Moodle. The accuracy score is published the next morning;
marks and comments come back before the next practice session.
:::

## 📊 Section 1 — EDA and visualisation (1 point)

You saw this series in Week 4. This time the plots have one job: to justify each letter of your
specification **before** `AutoETS` runs.

- A time plot, read for **trend**: is there one, and does it flatten (damping)?
- The **seasonal swing against the level** — one point per year, max minus min of the year against its
  mean. A flat cloud says additive season; a cloud that climbs with the level says multiplicative. The
  template gives you `swing_against_level()`.
- The validation split on a plot: history, validation window, your chosen model's forecast and 80%
  interval over it.
- One sentence per plot. **A plot with no reading attached earns nothing.**

## 🎯 Section 2 — Forecast accuracy (3 points)

Scored from your submission file, on the `h` observations after your history that nobody has seen.

$$
\text{skill} = \frac{\text{MASE of your forecast}}{\text{MASE of your benchmark}}
$$

| Skill | Points |
|---|---:|
| below 1 — you beat your benchmark | 3 |
| 1 to 1.1 — within 10% | 2 |
| above 1.1 | 1, and 3.3 must say why |

- **Your benchmark** is the best of the four simple methods — `mean`, `naive`, `snaive`, `drift` —
  by RMSE on the last `h` observations of your history, refitted on all of it. The template computes it
  by exactly the scorer's rule, so the number you see is the one you are compared against.
- **MASE** is scaled by the in-sample seasonal naive error of your whole history — the same `mase()` as
  in the template.
- You are never compared with your classmates.

::: {.callout-note}
## What the pool guarantees, and what it does not

Every series in the pool was issued only if **`AutoETS` fitted on the whole history beats its
benchmark** on the hidden horizon. That is a guarantee about `AutoETS` rerun on all of `y` — not about
every ETS model, and not about the letters `AutoETS` picked on `train`.

The Week 4 lecture's rule — shortlist on AICc, decide on a rolling origin — is still the right way to
work, and it is what 3.2 pays for. Measured on the whole pool: shortlisting the three best models by
AICc and choosing among them by a rolling origin beats the benchmark on **94%** of series and comes
within 10% on 98%; choosing by a rolling origin among everything, 85%. If your evidence leads you away
from `AutoETS`, follow it — and say in 3.2 what that evidence was.
:::

## ✍️ Section 3 — Justification block (3 points)

The part a human reads closely. Roughly a paragraph each, with numbers from your own cells.

| Item | Points | What earns them |
|---|---:|---|
| 3.1 | 1 | **Your specification, before the machine.** Each letter of `MY_SPEC` and the damping choice, tied to a plot from Section 1. What in the plots would have made you choose differently. |
| 3.2 | 1 | **What `AutoETS` chose, and what you submitted.** Where `AutoETS` agrees or disagrees with you, and why. Your shortlist with AICc and rolling MASE. The model you submitted and the evidence for it — and if it is not `AutoETS`'s choice, what made you leave it. |
| 3.3 | 1 | **What is left, and what you expect.** ACF and Ljung-Box on the **innovation** residuals, read: what structure is left and what it damages — the forecast or the interval. Your interval's coverage on the validation window. Your expected skill on the hidden horizon, and if you expect to lose, why. |

::: {.callout-important}
Marked on the reasoning. A specification by hand that `AutoETS` overrules, with a clear account of
why, scores full marks in 3.1 and 3.2. A model that wins and cannot say why it was chosen does not.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Where this goes wrong

- **Specifying after the fact.** `MY_SPEC` copied from `AutoETS` and justified backwards reads
  exactly like that. Write 3.1 from Section 1 alone.
- **Choosing on one window.** The validation window is one draw of `h` observations. In the practice
  session it ranked a damped model first; over three windows the same model was last of the shortlist.
- **Comparing AICc across transformations.** AICc is comparable between ETS models on the same `y`;
  not between `y` and `log(y)`, and not against anything that is not ETS.
- **`damped=None`.** With `model="AAA"` and no `damped`, `AutoETS` may return `ETS(A,Ad,A)`. The
  template's `fit_ets()` passes `damped` explicitly — use it.
- **Testing the wrong residuals.** Ljung-Box goes on `fit.model_["residuals"]` of the chosen model, not
  on `y`.
- **Forecasting from `train`.** The submission is refitted on the **whole** history.
- **Freezing `AutoETS`'s letters from `train`.** If you choose `AutoETS`, submit `fit_ets(y)` — the
  search rerun on all of `y`. On half the pool it lands on different letters than it did on `train`,
  and the guarantee is about the rerun, not about the letters it found first.
